answer:
Some studies report possible associations between microplastics in the body and gastrointestinal complications, inflammatory conditions, hormonal imbalances, and reproductive dysfunction [2]. Research published in 2021 showed high concentrations of microplastics in stool samples were associated with these outcomes [2]. Direct evidence linking microplastic exposure to adverse health outcomes in humans remains limited [2]. Human evidence is largely observational, reporting associations with biological markers rather than confirmed clinical outcomes [2]. A 2020 study found that only 38% of participants were convinced microplastics would be detrimental to human health [2].

Microplastics may induce inflammatory responses, oxidative stress, and cellular damage, contributing to various diseases [2]. Their surfaces can adsorb organic pollutants, heavy metals, and pathogenic microorganisms [1]. A systematic review confirmed widespread detection of microplastics and nanoplastics across human matrices, including respiratory secretions, systemic circulation, major organs, and placental tissue [3]. This detection underscores their ability to translocate within the human body [3]. That review did not report specific human health outcomes.
